mainTopic: No 'שלום' in the bathhouse, telling someone about a gift (the gift of שבת), and more teachings of רב through רבא בר מחסיא
overview: This amud opens by finishing a point from the previous page: a בית הכסא is unfit for prayer as soon as it is designated, because it is disgusting. The גמרא then rules that one may not greet with 'שלום' in a bathhouse, because שלום is an actual Name of ה׳. 'Faithful' (הימנותא), by contrast, only describes ה׳, so רב permits saying it in a bathroom. Through the same chain of teachers (רבא בר מחסיא in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב), the גמרא brings רב's rule that a giver must let the receiver know. This is learned from ה׳ telling משה about the gift of שבת, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applies it to giving bread to a child. The גמרא explains that telling is needed only when the gift would otherwise stay hidden, and the reward of שבת is exactly that kind of hidden gift. A story follows in which רב חסדא gives his priestly gifts to רבא בר מחסיא in exchange for רב's teachings. The amud ends with more teachings from the same chain: never favor one child over the others, as יוסף's coat shows, and prefer to live in a recently settled city, which רבי אבין derives from צוער. His proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The bathroom is different because it is disgusting
steps.stepSummary: This line finishes an answer from the previous page. It explains why a בית הכסא is treated more strictly than a בית המרחץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: A bathroom is different, because it is disgusting.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it started on the previous page. A בית הכסא becomes unfit for prayer as soon as it is set aside for that use, because it is a disgusting place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the גמרא was asking whether simply designating a place makes it unfit for תפלה. The answer is that a bathhouse only becomes a problem once people actually bathe there. A bathroom is different: just being called a bathroom makes it repulsive, so it is unfit right away.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the start of a new topic. It is the last line of an answer that began on the previous page (10a).

phrases.english: A bathroom is different
because it is disgusting.
phrases.notes: Once a place is called a bathroom, it is already repulsive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer to a question from 10a about whether designating a place affects its status.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Designating a bathhouse and designating a bathroom should have the same effect.
steps.terutzMaskana: A bathroom is disgusting from the moment it is designated. A bathhouse only becomes unfit once it is used.

steps.title: No greetings in the bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from the ברייתא (תוספתא) about the בית המרחץ: you may not greet people there.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no greeting of 'שלום' there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the teaching about the bathhouse: people do not greet each other with 'שלום' there. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא will use this line as support for an אמורא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line gives a rule without a reason. The reason will come in the next step. The word שלום is the key: it is the normal word for greeting someone, but it is also a Name of ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: There is not, in that place

phrases.english: There is no greeting of 'Shalom' there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the bathhouse teaching, now with a new rule about greetings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You may not greet another person with 'שלום' in a bathhouse.

steps.title: This supports רב המנונא: שלום is a Name of ה׳
steps.stepSummary: The line from the ברייתא supports רב המנונא, who said in the name of עולא that greeting someone in a bathhouse is forbidden because שלום is a Name of ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רב המנונא in the name of עולא, who said: A person may not greet his friend with 'שלום' in a bathhouse, because it says 'And he called Him: ה׳ שלום.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the ברייתא backs up רב המנונא. He also forbids saying 'שלום' in a bathhouse, and he gives the reason: שלום is one of ה׳'s Names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about גדעון's altar ('ה׳ שלום') shows that שלום is a Name of ה׳. A holy Name may not be said in an undignified place like a bathhouse. The ברייתא gave the rule, and רב המנונא gives the reason, so the two fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And he called Him: ה׳ שלום' (שופטים ו:כד)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the הלכה that one should not say 'שלום' as a greeting in a bathhouse or bathroom.

phrases.english: This supports Rav Hamnuna
in the name of Ulla, who said:
It is forbidden for a person to give 'Shalom'
to his friend in the bathhouse,
because it is said: 'And he called Him: ה׳ Shalom.'
phrases.notes: Gideon named the altar this way (Judges 6:24).

steps.triggerLanguage: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַב הַמְנוּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּעוּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא from step 2 as support for an אמורא.
steps.raayaObject: רב המנונא's rule that one may not greet with 'שלום' in a bathhouse

steps.title: Then 'faithful' should also be forbidden in a bathroom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reasoning: if a word used for ה׳ is forbidden, then 'faithfulness' (הימנותא) should also be forbidden, because ה׳ is called 'האל הנאמן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to this, saying 'faithfulness' should also be forbidden in a bathroom, since it is written: 'the faithful God.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes רב המנונא's reasoning further. If שלום is forbidden because it is connected to ה׳, then the word 'faithful' should be forbidden too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge says the reasoning proves too much. Many ordinary words, like 'faithful', appear in פסוקים describing ה׳. If every such word were forbidden in a bathroom, the rule would become far too broad.

phrases.english: But according to this
'faithfulness' should also be forbidden to say in a bathroom,
since it is written: 'The faithful God.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning behind רב המנונא's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reasoning that שלום is forbidden because it is linked to ה׳
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Taken to its logical end, the reasoning would also forbid 'faithful', which seems unreasonable.

steps.title: רב explicitly permits saying 'faithfulness' in a bathroom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks the reply 'Yes, that is also forbidden' by quoting רב, who explicitly permits saying הימנותא in a bathroom.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say 'Yes, it really is forbidden,' didn't רבא בר מחסיא say in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב: It is permitted to say 'faithfulness' in a bathroom!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא expects the reply 'Yes, faithfulness is also forbidden.' It shuts that reply down by quoting רב, who said that saying הימנותא in a bathroom is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This makes the challenge much stronger. It is no longer just a question of logic, because there is an actual ruling that permits הימנותא. So the גמרא must now explain how שלום is different from הימנותא.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say, 'Yes, that is so'

phrases.english: And if you say that it is indeed so,
but didn't Rava bar Machseya say,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא, אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Chama bar Gurya said, Rav said:
It is permitted to say 'faithfulness' in a bathroom!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge in step 4 by ruling out the easy answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible reply that הימנותא is also forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב explicitly permits הימנותא, so the reasoning behind forbidding שלום must be explained some other way.

steps.title: שלום is an actual Name; 'faithful' only describes ה׳
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that נאמן is only a description of ה׳, while שלום is an actual Name of ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, ה׳'s Name itself is not called that, since we translate it as 'the faithful God.' Here, ה׳'s Name itself is called שלום, as it is written: 'And he called Him: ה׳ שלום.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. 'Faithful' is just a word that describes ה׳, but שלום is one of His actual Names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from the תרגום, which renders 'האל הנאמן' as 'אלהא מהימנא', the God who is faithful. That shows 'faithful' is only an adjective. In the פסוק about גדעון, however, 'ה׳ שלום' is the Name itself, so שלום has the holiness of a Name.

keyTerms.meaning: As we translate it (in the תרגום)

steps.whatToRemember: A word that only describes ה׳, like 'faithful', may be said in a bathroom. A word that is an actual Name of ה׳, like שלום, may not.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם שֵׁם גּוּפֵיהּ לָא אִיקְּרִי הָכִי,
phrases.english: There, the Name itself is not called that,
since we translate it as 'the faithful God,'
phrases.notes: It is a description, not a Name.

phrases.english: here, the Name itself is called 'Shalom'
as it is written: 'And he called Him: ה׳ Shalom.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם שֵׁם גּוּפֵיהּ לָא אִיקְּרִי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in steps 4 and 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between a Name and a description
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any word used about ה׳ should be forbidden in a bathroom.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a word that is itself a Name of ה׳, like שלום, is forbidden.

steps.title: One who gives a gift must let the receiver know
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain of rabbis: a person who gives a gift must tell the receiver. The source is the pasuk about שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא בר מחסיא said in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב: One who gives a gift to his friend must let him know, as it says: 'To know that I am ה׳ who makes you holy.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. Since it just quoted this chain of rabbis, it brings another teaching they said: when you give someone a gift, let them know it came from you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pasuk about שבת says 'to know', which shows that ה׳ wanted the Jewish people to know about His gift. From this we learn that a giver should make sure the receiver knows about the gift. Doing so builds love between people.

keyTerms.meaning: 'To know that I am ה׳ who makes you holy' (שמות לא:יג)

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new topic, not part of the bathroom discussion. It appears here only because it was said by the same chain of rabbis.

phrases.english: And Rava bar Machseya said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Chama bar Gurya said, Rav said:
One who gives a gift to his friend must let him know.
As it is said: 'To know that I am ה׳ who makes you holy.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא בַּר מַחְסֵיָא אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching brought because it comes from the same chain of transmission as step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who gives a gift must let the receiver know about it.

steps.title: A ברייתא: שבת is ה׳'s hidden gift
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports רב‎: ה׳ told משה that He has a precious gift called שבת and told him to go let the Jewish people know.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא also teaches this: 'To know that I am ה׳ who makes you holy.' ה׳ said to משה: I have a good gift in My treasure house, and its name is שבת. I want to give it to ישראל. Go let them know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as רב. It explains the pasuk as ה׳ telling משה to inform the Jewish people about the gift of שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spells out how the pasuk teaches רב's rule. Even ה׳, when giving a gift, made sure the receivers were told about it. Inform the receiver is exactly what רב said.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He

phrases.english: A baraita also teaches this:
'To know that I am ה׳ who makes you holy,'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:

phrases.aramaic: מַתָּנָה טוֹבָה יֵשׁ לִי בְּבֵית גְּנָזַי וְשַׁבָּת שְׁמָהּ,
phrases.english: I have a good gift in My treasure house, and its name is Shabbat,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲנִי מְבַקֵּשׁ לִיתְּנָהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, לֵךְ וְהוֹדִיעָם.
phrases.english: and I want to give it to Israel. Go and let them know.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's teaching from step 7 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that a giver must inform the receiver
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא explaining that ה׳ told משה to inform ישראל about the gift of שבת

steps.title: Giving bread to a child: let the mother know
steps.stepSummary: From this source, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל teaches that one who gives bread to a child must let the child's mother know.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: One who gives bread to a child must let his mother know.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applies the gift rule to a practical case. If you give a small child some bread, make sure the mother finds out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small child cannot really appreciate who gave him the gift. So the mother should be told instead, and the good feelings the gift creates will reach her.

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל:
phrases.english: From here Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:

phrases.aramaic: הַנּוֹתֵן פַּת לְתִינוֹק, צָרִיךְ לְהוֹדִיעַ לְאִמּוֹ.
phrases.english: One who gives bread to a child must let his mother know.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical rule from the ברייתא in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who gives bread to a child must let the mother know.

steps.title: How should he let the mother know?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical thing the giver should do to the child so the mother will find out.
steps.simpleTranslation: What should he do to the child?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question: how does the giver make sure the mother finds out? It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The giver may not be able to tell the mother himself. So the question is how to leave a sign on the child that will make the mother ask.

keyTerms.meaning: What should he do to him?

phrases.english: What should he do to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to carry out the rule from step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical way to inform the mother

steps.title: אביי: put oil or eye-paint on the child
steps.stepSummary: אביי says to smear oil on the child or put כוחל (eye-paint) around his eyes, so the mother will ask about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: He should smear oil on him, or fill his eyes with eye-paint.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a practical method: leave a visible mark on the child. When the mother asks about it, the child will tell her who was kind to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mark itself does not inform the mother. It only makes her curious, so she asks, and then she hears about the gift.

phrases.english: Abaye said: He smears oil on him,
or fills his eyes with eye-paint.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Leave a visible mark of oil or eye-paint on the child, so the mother asks about it.

steps.title: What about today, when we worry about witchcraft?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what to do nowadays, when a mother might fear that oil or eye-paint from a stranger is witchcraft.
steps.simpleTranslation: And nowadays, when we are worried about witchcraft, what should he do?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a practical problem with אביי's method. Today people fear that a stranger putting oil or eye-paint on a child might be doing כשפים (witchcraft). This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's sign could backfire. Instead of the mother feeling grateful, she might become frightened. So a different kind of sign is needed.

phrases.english: And nowadays, when we are concerned about witchcraft, what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out a problem with אביי's method in present-day conditions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A sign that will not frighten the mother as possible witchcraft

steps.title: רב פפא: smear him with the same food
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says to smear a little of the same food that was given on the child, so the mother will notice and ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: He should smear on him some of that same kind of food.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a safer sign: smear a bit of the food itself on the child. The mother will notice, ask, and find out about the gift without any fear of witchcraft.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food is harmless and has nothing to do with witchcraft. It also shows the mother exactly what the child was given. This solves the problem from step 12 while keeping the goal of letting the mother know.
steps.whatToRemember: A giver should let the receiver know about a gift, just as ה׳ told ישראל about שבת. For a small child, let the mother know, today by smearing a little of the food itself on the child.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: שָׁאֵיף לֵיהּ מֵאוֹתוֹ הַמִּין.
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: He smears on him some of that same kind (of food).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא שָׁאֵיף לֵיהּ מֵאוֹתוֹ הַמִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Smear some of the same food on the child, which avoids any fear of witchcraft.

steps.title: Challenge: A giver does not need to tell
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule using רב חמא ברבי חנינא, who says a giver does not need to tell the receiver, as seen with משה's glowing face.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? Didn't רב חמא ברבי חנינא say: One who gives a gift to his friend does not need to tell him, as it says: 'And משה did not know that the skin of his face was glowing while He spoke with him'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's rule from Step 7 (you must tell the person about a gift), which רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applied in Step 9, by quoting a teacher who says the exact opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ gave משה a glowing face, a real gift, yet משה did not know about it. So ה׳ did not tell him. That suggests a giver does not need to tell, which seems to clash with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: The skin of his face glowed

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Rav Ḥama son of Rabbi Ḥanina say:
phrases.notes: The brackets show a corrected version of the name.

phrases.english: One who gives a gift to his friend
does not need to inform him,
as it says: 'And Moses did not know'
that the skin of his face shone
when He spoke with him'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי וְהָאָמַר רַב חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the core rule of Step 9 and challenges it with a conflicting teaching.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule (step 7) that a giver must tell the receiver, which רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applied to bread for a child (step 9).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A gift from ה׳ to משה was given without telling him, which shows telling is not required.

steps.title: Answer: It depends whether the gift will become known
steps.stepSummary: No contradiction: a gift that will become known on its own needs no telling; a gift that would stay hidden must be told.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. This one (no need to tell) is about something that will become known anyway. That one (must tell) is about something that will not become known.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash by splitting the two rules into two different kinds of gifts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's glowing face would surely be noticed and he would find out, so no announcement was needed. The bread given to a child (Step 9) would not be discovered by the mother unless she is told, so the giver must tell.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is about a matter that is likely to be revealed,
that is about a matter that is not likely to be revealed.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּמִילְּתָא דַּעֲבִידָא לְאִגַּלּוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא by type of gift)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two teachings seemed to argue about whether a giver must ever tell.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are right: tell when the gift would stay hidden; no need when it will come out on its own.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule: if the gift will be discovered anyway, no need to tell; if it won't, you must tell.

steps.title: Challenge: שבת would have become known anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: שבת would become known with the other מצוות, so why did ה׳ tell משה to announce it as a gift?
steps.simpleTranslation: But שבת is something that would become known anyway!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the new rule against the source verse about שבת (from earlier steps), which seemed to need an announcement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the rule of Step 15, a gift that will be revealed needs no announcement. שבת would be taught to the people with all the other מצוות anyway, so the special order to 'let them know' seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: The Shabbat, described as a gift from ה׳

phrases.english: But Shabbat,
is it not likely to be revealed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the answer of Step 15 to raise a new difficulty from the שבת verse.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of Step 15 as applied to the שבת verse.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If revealed gifts need no announcing, the announcing of שבת is hard to explain.

steps.title: Answer: The reward of שבת is hidden
steps.stepSummary: שבת itself would be known, but its reward would not, so it needed to be announced.
steps.simpleTranslation: The giving of its reward is not something that would become known.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the hidden part of the gift is the reward for keeping שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The day of שבת is public, but how great its reward is cannot be seen. Since that part would stay hidden, ה׳ told משה to let the people know, which fits the rule of Step 15.

phrases.english: The giving of its reward
is not likely to be revealed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying a hidden part of the gift
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שבת seemed to be a fully public gift.
steps.terutzMaskana: Its reward is hidden, so announcing it was needed.
steps.whatToRemember: שבת itself is known, but its reward is hidden, so it had to be announced.

steps.title: רב חסדא's offer for a new teaching of רב
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא held two priestly gifts from an ox and offered them to anyone who brought him a new teaching in the name of רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא was holding in his hand two מתנות כהונה from an ox. He said: Anyone who comes and tells me a new teaching in the name of רב, I will give these to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story. It is setting up how another teaching about gifts was brought in the name of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא was a כהן and so received מתנות from slaughtered animals. He loved רב's teachings so much that he offered these as a prize. This sets up the next step, where someone wins the prize.

keyTerms.meaning: Priestly gifts from an ox (shoulder, cheeks, stomach)

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda was holding in his hand
two priestly gifts from an ox,
he said: Anyone who comes
and tells me a new teaching
in the name of Rav
I will give them to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא הֲוָה נָקֵיט בִּידֵיהּ תַּרְתֵּי מַתְּנָתָא דְתוֹרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a story connected to the topic of telling about gifts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב חסדא promises his priestly gifts for any new teaching of רב.

steps.title: רבא בר מחסיא brings רב's teaching and wins the gift
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר מחסיא quotes רב: a giver must tell the receiver, from the שבת verse. רב חסדא gives him the gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר מחסיא said to him: This is what רב said: One who gives a gift to his friend must let him know, as it says: 'To know that I am ה׳ Who makes you holy.' He gave it to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר מחסיא shares a teaching of רב and receives the prize.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the very teaching of רב already quoted in Step 7, and here we see how רבא בר מחסיא first reported it, as a 'new' teaching for רב חסדא. Fittingly, רב חסדא gives a gift right after hearing a teaching about gifts.

keyTerms.meaning: To know that I am ה׳ Who sanctifies you (said about שבת)

phrases.english: Rava bar Meḥasseya said to him,
Rav said as follows:
One who gives a gift to his friend
needs to inform him.
As it says: 'To know'
that I am God Who sanctifies you.'
He gave it to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא בַּר מַחְסֵיָא, הָכִי אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fulfills the offer made in Step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: a giver must let the receiver know, learned from the שבת verse.

steps.title: Are רב's teachings so dear to you?
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר מחסיא asks רב חסדא whether רב's teachings are really that precious to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Are רב's teachings so beloved to you?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר מחסיא asks a question that sets up his next teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is surprised that רב חסדא would give away valuable gifts just for a teaching. The question prepares him to share a saying of רב about people valuing what they understand.

phrases.english: He said: Are they beloved to you,
the teachings of Rav, so much?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר חֲבִיבִין עֲלָךְ שְׁמַעְתָּתָא דְּרַב כּוּלֵּי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to רב חסדא giving the gift.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב's teachings are truly that precious to רב חסדא.

steps.title: רב חסדא answers: Yes
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא confirms that רב's teachings are that dear to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Yes.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא simply answers yes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His short answer shows how much he valued רב's Torah. It opens the door for רבא בר מחסיא to share another teaching.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, רב's teachings are that precious to him.

steps.title: רב's saying: Fine wool is precious to those who wear it
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר מחסיא shares another saying of רב: fine wool is valued by those who wear it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רב said: Fine wool is precious to those who wear it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר מחסיא shares a second teaching of רב that fits the moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only someone used to fine wool can appreciate how good it is. So too, only a great scholar like רב חסדא can truly appreciate how precious רב's teachings are.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what [he] meant when he said
Precious to those who wear it

phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rav said:
Fine wool is precious to those who wear it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב חסדא's 'yes' with a fitting saying.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only one who knows quality can truly value it.

steps.title: רב חסדא loves the second teaching even more
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא is delighted, says the second teaching is better than the first, and wishes he had another gift to give.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Did רב say that?! The last one is better to me than the first, and if I were holding another gift, I would give it to you.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with רב חסדא's excited reaction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new saying explained his own love of Torah, so it meant even more to him. This closes the story.

phrases.english: He said to him: Rav said this?!
The latter is preferable to me than the first,
and if I were holding another,
I would give it to you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reaction to Step 22, closing the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב חסדא valued רב's Torah so much that he would give more gifts for it.

steps.title: Never favor one child over the others
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches not to treat one child better than his brothers; the extra fine wool יעקב gave יוסף led to jealousy and going down to מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא בר מחסיא said in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב: A person should never treat one son differently from the other sons. Because of two סלעים' weight of fine wool that יעקב gave יוסף more than his other sons, his brothers became jealous, one thing led to another, and our fathers went down to מצרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רב from the same chain, linked to the word מילת (fine wool).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small extra gift, the special coat, sparked jealousy. That jealousy led to selling יוסף and finally to the whole family going down to מצרים. A tiny favoritism can cause huge results.

keyTerms.meaning: The weight of two סלעים (small amount)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic lesson in parenting and fairness taken straight from the story of יוסף.

phrases.english: And Rava bar Meḥasseya said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: that Rav Ḥama bar Gurya said that Rav said:
A person should never distinguish
his son from among the sons,
for because of the weight of two sela of fine wool
that Jacob gave to Joseph
more than the rest of his sons,
his brothers became jealous of him
and the matter unfolded
and our forefathers went down to Egypt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא בַּר מַחְסֵיָא אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching from the same chain (רבא בר מחסיא), connected by the theme of fine wool.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not favor one child over the others.

steps.title: Live in a recently settled city
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches to look for a city that was settled recently, because it has fewer sins, citing לוט's words about צוער.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא בר מחסיא said in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב: A person should always seek to live in a city whose settling is recent, because since it was settled recently, its sins are few. As it says: 'Behold this city is close to flee there, and it is small.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רב from the same chain, with a verse as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A new city has not had time to build up many sins. רב reads 'קרובה' in לוט's words as 'recently settled' and 'מצער' as 'few sins'. The next step explains why this reading is needed.

phrases.english: And Rava bar Meḥasseya said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: that Rav Ḥama bar Gurya said that Rav said:
A person should always seek and dwell
in a city whose settling is recent,
since because its settling is recent
its sins are few.
As it says: 'Behold, here is this city'
that is close to flee there
and it is small.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא בַּר מַחְסֵיָא אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב: לְעוֹלָם יְחַזֵּר אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching from the same chain of transmission (after steps 5, 7 and 24).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Prefer living in a newly settled city, since it has fewer sins.

steps.title: What does 'close' mean in the verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'קרובה' means, and rejects the simple meaning 'close in distance', since the angels could see that.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'close' mean? If you say it means close by and small, but they could see it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks רב's reading by asking what the word 'close' means, and pushes away the simple meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If לוט only meant the city was nearby and small, why say it? The angels could see that for themselves. So 'close' must mean something that cannot be seen.

keyTerms.meaning: What is / What does it mean
That it is near and small

phrases.english: What is 'close'?
If you say: close, meaning near and small
but they could see it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Examines the verse used as the source in Step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The true meaning of 'קרובה' in the verse.

steps.title: It means recently settled, so its sins are few
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes 'close' means recently settled, and therefore its sins are few.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, because its settling was recent, its sins were few.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct meaning of the verse, which supports רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since 'near and small' adds nothing, 'קרובה' must mean the city was settled recently, and 'מצער' means its sins were few. That is exactly רב's teaching.

phrases.english: Rather, because its settling was recent,
its sins were few.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Close' means recently settled, which is why its sins were few.

steps.title: רבי אבין's proof from the word 'נא'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין proves צוער was newer than סדום: 'נא' equals 51 in גימטריא, while סדום was 52 years old. The text continues on the next daf.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבין said: What is the verse? As it is written: 'Let me escape there, please (נא).' The גימטריא of 'נא' is fifty-one, while סדום was fifty-two. And its tranquility...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבין brings a verse showing that צוער was settled later than סדום. This passage stops in the middle of his explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The letters נ (50) and א (1) make 51, hinting that צוער was 51 years old. סדום was 52, so צוער was one year newer and had fewer sins. The word 'וְשַׁלְוָתָהּ' begins the next part of the proof.
steps.confusionAlert: The word 'וְשַׁלְוָתָהּ' is the start of a sentence that finishes on the next daf; don't try to make sense of it alone here.

phrases.english: Rabbi Avin said: What is the verse?
As it is written: 'Let me escape there, please.'
'Na' in numerical value
is fifty-one,
and that of Sodom was fifty-two.
And its tranquility

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a verse proving that צוער was more recently settled, supporting Step 27.
steps.raayaObject: That צוער was settled more recently than סדום.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'נא' in בראשית יט:כ, numerical value 51, compared with סדום's 52 years.
